reference_answer: Because it is evidence of distress. As the bench book explains, recently, courts have accepted that distress at the time of making a complaint can be admitted. This is because distress has probative value in inferring a causal link between the alleged victim’s reaction and the likelihood an offence occurred, as well as enhancing the credibility of the complainant if a causal connection can be inferred.

question: Mia receives several late-night calls from Noah. Each time she answers, he says nothing. Knowing his violent history, she believes he is outside about to attack. What is the citation of the common law case that held this conduct can amount to assault?
reference_answer: The citation/case explicitly referenced in the bench book is R v Ireland [1998] AC 147.

question: A 13-year-old, Hamish, orders a rideshare to a friend’s house after a fight with his parents. The driver, Zoe, picks him up outside his home, asks “Are your parents okay with you going?”, gets a vague shrug, but offers no encouragement and simply follows the entered destination. On these facts, has Zoe taken Hamish away?
reference_answer: No. Zoe has not “taken Hamish away” because she was not an effective cause of his leaving, but merely a peripheral, incidental means of transport. The bench book explains that this element requires the accused to take an active part in the child’s departure, such as by offering inducements or persuasion, which Zoe did not do here.
hyde_text: Zoe is a driver and cannot be taken away.
